story.kicker: Mission 1 · The Moon, de Gerlache rim
story.site: REL's first rover goes to the rim of de Gerlache crater, near the lunar south pole. Some crater floors near the pole never see the Sun and can be as cold as about −248 °C; in 2009, NASA's LCROSS probe struck one of them, Cabeus crater, and found water in the debris. NASA has named a region on the de Gerlache rim as a candidate landing region for its Artemis III crewed mission.
sources: NASA SVS 11230, Diviner temperatures of the lunar poles (svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/11230)
Colaprete et al. (2010), Detection of water in the LCROSS ejecta plume, Science 330:463, doi:10.1126/science.1186986
NASA release 24-136, NASA provides update on Artemis III Moon landing regions (nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-provides-update-on-artemis-iii-moon-landing-regions/)

speedInfo: The mission compresses 14 days of lunar daylight into 5 minutes. Driving is compressed too: rovers in this game drive {compression} times faster than the real speeds their parts are modeled on.

On Apollo 15 in 1971, the crew reported that about 6 to 7 km/h was the most comfortable driving speed for the Lunar Roving Vehicle. Its top speed was of the order of 9 to 13 km/h, depending on slope, roughness, and soil.
Robotic rovers drive far slower. NASA's Curiosity and Perseverance rovers on Mars have a top speed of about 4 cm/s (0.15 km/h) on flat ground.

design.speedInfoSources: Sources: NASA TR R-401, Mobility Performance of the Lunar Roving Vehicle (1972); NASA/JPL Mars Science Laboratory and Mars 2020 press kits.

history.survived: India's Pragyan rover did likewise in 2023: it completed its planned one lunar day of operations, about 14 Earth days, before ISRO put it into sleep mode for the lunar night.
history.energy: NASA's solar-powered Opportunity rover ended the same way: a Mars-wide dust storm covered its site, its last signal arrived on June 10, 2018, and NASA declared the mission over on February 13, 2019.
history.stuck: NASA's Spirit rover met this fate on Mars: it became stuck in soft soil on May 1, 2009, and in January 2010 NASA redefined its mission as a stationary science platform.
history.froze: India's Vikram lander and Pragyan rover entered sleep mode before the cold lunar night in September 2023, and ISRO has not reported regaining contact after its wake-up attempts around September 22.
history.destroyed: The Soviet Lunokhod 2 rover was also lost to damage: its lid touched a crater wall on May 9, 1973, dust fell onto its radiator, it overheated, and the mission was closed on June 4, 1973.
history.rollover: No planetary rover is known to have been lost to a rollover. NASA's Spirit rover had a static tip-over angle of 45 degrees, and its software stopped a drive whenever its tilt passed a set limit.

design.title: Welcome to REL
body: The Rover Exploration Laboratory (REL) designs and operates robotic rovers for planetary exploration. To transport a rover to the planetary surface, REL must purchase a launch ticket, reserving space aboard a launch vehicle.
As a rover engineer, you are responsible for rover design, launch preparation, and surface operations.

design.title: Mission funding
body: Each mission has a designated budget covering rover components and launch costs. Completing milestones during surface operations generates revenue.
To qualify for the next mission, the final balance must meet or exceed the **pass mark**. If the balance falls short, the mission must be repeated.

design.title: Rover design
body: Configure the four required components: **frame, wheels, power, and battery**. You may then equip optional scientific instruments in the payload bay.
Each instrument consumes energy both during operation (**active**) and while switched on (**standby**). Instrument cards display energy requirements and the milestones each instrument can earn.
Each component has **cost, mass, and size**. The specification sheet calculates the combined totals for your rover.

drive.title: Driving and time
body: W A S D or arrow keys to drive. Space to brake.
The mission lasts {minutes} minutes, which represent {days} days of lunar daylight. There is no clock: time is read from the Sun, which circles low on the horizon, and from the moving shadows.

drive.title: Energy
body: The energy bar is the battery. The solar panel charges it only in sunlight; the readout under the meters shows "{sunlit}" or "{shadow}".
Driving uses more energy than the panel earns. Stop in sunlight to recharge. At zero energy the mission ends.

drive.title: Damage and cold
body: Hard impacts and ground steeper than {maxSlope}° damage the rover. A rollover ends the mission at once.
Inside permanent shadow the cold meter rises, and the rover freezes when it is full. Lights are required to enter permanent shadow; a heater slows freezing.

drive.title: Solar flares
body: When a solar flare is detected, a warning bar appears {warningSeconds} seconds before it strikes.
Before the bar runs out, power down with P or move into shadow. A powered-down rover cannot drive, but its panel still charges.

drive.title: Instruments and map

instrument.camera: Camera: {key} (or its button) takes a photograph. Photographs count toward milestones at viewpoints, or with Earth above the horizon in view at least {earthMinDistance} m from the lander.
instrument.drill: Drill: stop the rover, then press {key} (or its button) to drill a regolith sample. Samples count at up to three sites, each at least {sampleSpacing} m from the lander and from each other.
instrument.neutron: Neutron spectrometer: {key} (or its button) switches it on or off. While on, a hydrogen meter beside the meters reads the ground as the rover drives, and it draws a little energy.
instrument.xray: X-ray spectrometer: stop beside a boulder, then press {key} (or its button) to read the rock's main elements.
instrument.seismometer: Seismometer station: stop and press {key} (or its button) to set it down before the moonquake. Stations count only more than {stationMinDistance} m from the lander; closer in, the key must be pressed twice.
instrument.reflector: Laser retroreflector: stop where Earth is in view (the Earth light beside the meters) and press {key} (or its button) to set it down. Stations count only more than {stationMinDistance} m from the lander; closer in, the key must be pressed twice.

body: Each instrument in the payload bay has a number key, 1 to {bayMax} in bay order, and a button beside the meters.
The engineering notebook records what the mission teaches about the rover. Open it with N or the Notebook button; the mission pauses while it is open, and Escape closes it.

The map starts zoomed in on the lander and widens as the rover explores. It shows only ground within {revealRadius} m of where the rover has been, and sites appear once the rover finds them. Arrows at the edge of the map point toward the orbital survey leads from the landing briefing.

credits.heading: Data sources and credits
credits.intro: The terrain, lighting, ground imagery, solar flares and facts in Rover Engineer come from the published sources below.
credits.disclaimer: REL (Rover Exploration Laboratory) is a fictional agency. Rover Engineer is an entry to the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 and is not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA.
credits.generated: The star field and the boulders are generated by the game's own rules, not taken from a data set. The rolled boulder and its track, the hydrogen-rich ground and each site's rock types are placed by design, inspired by the findings credited under the milestone facts; they were not observed at these spots. The cold traps and young craters are found in the NASA terrain and lighting layers credited above.
